query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small reactive alloying element that forms stable lubricious oxides—specifically, incorporating about 2–5 at.% vanadium into the CoCrFeNi matrix—will trigger the in‐situ development of a continuous, protective oxide tribolayer. This layer is expected to stabilize the friction and wear behavior over a sliding temperature range spanning from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, homogenized CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix in its as‐processed state.
generation.intervention: Introduce 2–5 at.% vanadium as a minor reactive alloying addition into the CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed under ambient, oxidizing conditions with a continuous temperature sweep from ~25 °C to 800 °C and under representative normal loads that simulate real tribological contact stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent tribolayer comprised primarily of lubricious vanadium oxide (e.g., V2O5) along with native oxide species from Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni.
generation.mechanism: The vanadium addition promotes localized oxidation during sliding. The resulting vanadium oxide phase has lubricious properties at room temperature and remains thermally stable at elevated temperatures. This in‐situ generated, self‐renewing glaze layer continuously protects the sliding interface from excessive adhesive and abrasive wear, thus maintaining a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the vanadium-doped alloy is predicted to show a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient and a consistently reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which exhibits increased friction and wear at either end of the temperature range due to insufficient self-lubricating phase formation at low temperatures and non-protective tribolayer formation at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 25 °C to 800 °C; Environment: Ambient oxidizing atmosphere; Load: Normal loads typically used in sliding tribological tests.
generation.uncertainty: Exact vanadium concentration and the detailed phase assemblage of the tribolayer under dynamic sliding conditions may vary. Optimization of the processing parameters is necessary to ensure consistent formation of the desired lubricious oxides.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one consisting of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another with the optimized 3 at.% vanadium addition. Subject both sample sets to identical sliding wear tests in an ambient oxidizing atmosphere over a temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C at controlled normal loads and sliding speeds. Post-test, analyze the worn surfaces using SEM, EDS, and XRD to assess tribolayer formation and composition.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (µ) as a function of temperature
Wear rate (calculating wear volume per normal load and sliding distance)
Microstructural and compositional analyses of the in-situ formed tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the V-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 20% reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the complete temperature range) compared to the baseline, or if the expected lubricious vanadium oxide phase is absent or unstable in the tribolayer analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. In order to address to these important technical issues that HEAs are currently facing, we proposed here to use the eutectic alloy idea to design HEAs with the composite structure, or it can be said to use the high-entropy alloy concept to design eutectic alloys. Furthermore, we proposed to design the eutectic alloys with a mixture of soft fcc and hard bcc phases, to achieve the balance of high fracture strength and high ductility. Apart from being a new way to obtain the composite structure in HEAs, eutectic alloys are also known to be good candidate high-temperature alloys, because the eutectic solidification structure has the following features: 1) near-equilibrium microstructures that resist change at temperatures as high as their reaction temperature; 2) low-energy phase boundaries; 3) controllable microstructures; 4) high rupture strength; 5) stable defect structures; 6) good high-temperature creep resistance; 7) regular lamellar or rod-like eutectic organization, forming an in-situ composite. frame.system: The starting system is a bulk CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix in its as-processed (e.g., homogenized) state used for sliding wear evaluation.
frame.goal: Achieve and maintain a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across a very broad temperature range—from room temperature (~25°C) up to 800°C—during sliding contact.
frame.limitation: The current CoCrFeNi alloy shows performance degradation (i.e., increased friction and wear) at one or both ends of the wide temperature range, due to changes in surface reaction kinetics and the evolution of the tribolayer under sliding.
root_cause_cues: maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range
difficulty of maintaining low friction and wear under these conditions
constraints: A single intervention that can operate effectively across the entire temperature range
Must specify temperature (room temperature to 800°C), load, and environmental (e.g., oxidizing ambient) conditions
The intervention must be compared directly with the performance of the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy
The proposed mechanism must be operative continuously over mechano-thermal transitions
A controlled falsification experiment is required
frame.regime: Sliding wear tests conducted under ambient (oxidizing) conditions over a temperature sweep from ~25°C to 800°C with defined normal loads replicating real tribological contact stresses.
prior_attempts: Conventional approaches based on surface coatings or dual-phase modifications have only provided limited success by addressing either low- or high-temperature regimes separately.
Standard CoCrFeNi alloys without additional elements tend to form non-protective tribolayers at high temperatures, while at lower temperatures insufficient self-lubricant phases develop.

families.principle: Altering the alloy’s bulk chemical composition to enable in‐situ formation of beneficial, self‐lubricating and thermally stable phases (or oxides) that continuously form a protective tribolayer across the full temperature range.
cues_for: maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range
insufficient self-lubricant phases at lower temperature and non‐protective tribolayer formation at high temperature
cues_against: Prior approaches with surface coatings and dual-phase modifications have only addressed isolated temperature regimes
families.best_lever: Introduce a minor reactive alloying addition (e.g., a small percentage of an element that forms stable, lubricious oxides at both low and high temperatures) to the CoCrFeNi matrix, triggering continuous in‐situ tribolayer self-generation.

families.principle: Using controlled heat or thermomechanical treatments to induce precipitations, phase transformations, or residual stress states that optimize surface or bulk properties under sliding conditions.
cues_for: the broad test regime (room temperature to 800°C) invites the idea that tailored heat treatments might create phases active across the entire temperature range
cues_against: A static pre-treatment may not continuously adapt to changing mechanical and thermal conditions during sliding, which is critical for performance
families.best_lever: Design a sequential annealing protocol that induces a population of self-lubricating precipitates or stable phases capable of evolving with temperature.

families.principle: Engineering the internal microstructure—such as grain size gradients, nano-/micro-scale phase distributions, or precipitate networks—to enhance load-bearing capacity and promote favorable tribolayer evolution.
cues_for: performance degradation attributed to tribolayer evolution hints that a controlled microstructural architecture might better manage stress and oxidation kinetics
cues_against: The starting material is a homogenized state; altering the architecture might improve local responses, but it is not as directly implicated in continuous, broad temperature protection as bulk compositional changes
families.best_lever: Introduce a gradient microstructure with a fine distribution of nano-precipitates to stabilize the formation and retention of a protective tribolayer during sliding.

families.principle: Modifying processing conditions (such as melt processing, rapid solidification, or chemical synthesis routes) to tailor phase distributions and defect structures, which in turn can influence tribological performance.
cues_for: starting system is an as-processed, homogenized state, suggesting room to improve via processing adjustments
cues_against: There is no explicit cue suggesting that altering synthesis alone will remedy the full temperature span issue, and prior attempts have focused on compositional or coating interventions
families.best_lever: Adopt a rapid solidification technique to refine grain structure and promote metastable phase formation that may enhance tribolayer stability during sliding.

families.principle: Modifying or engineering the surface and its interfaces (via coatings, treatments or in-situ generated films) to tailor interfacial reactions and frictional behavior during contact.
cues_for: the issue of non-protective tribolayers and high friction points to surface reaction kinetics and the role of the sliding interface
cues_against: Conventional approaches based on surface coatings have been mentioned as having only limited success by addressing isolated temperature regimes rather than the continuous mechano-thermal transitions required here
families.best_lever: Develop an adaptive, in-situ forming self-healing tribofilm via engineered surface treatments that actively respond to the temperature changes during sliding.
